summary: Defines the Authority Information Access CRL extension, which provides a way to discover and retrieve the certificates of CRL issuers. It uses the same syntax as the certificate extension in RFC 3280, which it updates. It is on the standards track and was later replaced by RFC 5280.

eli5.summary: A note on a revoked-certificate list saying where to find the person who signed it, so you can check it.

questions: how to find crl issuer certificate
subtitle: Helping applications find CRL issuer certificates for certificate revocation checking.

tldr.problem: When validating a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) to check if a certificate was revoked, applications need to build a path from the CRL issuer back to a trusted root, but finding the CRL issuer's certificate can be difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4325 allows CRLs to include an Authority Information Access extension that points to locations where CRL issuer certificates can be found, using the same syntax and mechanism already defined for certificates in RFC 3280.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use the information in the CRL itself to discover and retrieve the certificates they need to validate that the CRL is genuine and trustworthy.

today: RFC 4325 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3280. It was itself superseded by RFC 5280, which consolidated and updated the X.509 PKI standards. The core mechanism remains valid for CRL implementations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3280 specifies how to validate certification paths and how to determine whether a certificate has been revoked. One revocation checking mechanism is the Certificate Revocation List (CRL). RFC 3280 also specifies how to validate a CRL, which involves constructing a valid certification path from the signer of the CRL to a trust anchor.

Building a CRL issuer certification path is straightforward when the certificate of the CRL issuer is already present in the certification path associated with the target certificate. However, it can be complex in other situations. There are several legitimate scenarios where the CRL issuer's certificate is not readily available or easily discovered, such as when indirect CRLs are used, when a Certification Authority changes its certificate signing key, or when the CA employs separate keys for certificate signing and CRL signing.
sections.eli5: When you check if a certificate is broken, you look at a list signed by someone. You need to make sure that someone is real. Sometimes it is easy to find their proof, sometimes it is hard.

sections.title: Existing Discovery Methods
sections.content:
Current methods for finding the certificate of a CRL issuer include directory lookup and the Subject Information Access extension. Directory lookup requires the existence and maintenance of a directory that has been populated with all necessary certificates. The Subject Information Access extension, found in intermediary CA certificates, supports building the CRL issuer certification path top-down from a trust anchor, but this requires that some certificates in the CRL issuer path include an appropriate Subject Information Access extension.

RFC 3280 already provides for bottom-up discovery through the Authority Information Access extension, where the id-ad-caIssuers access method can specify one or more access locations that reference CA certificates. This document extends that capability to CRLs themselves, enabling CRL checking applications to use the same access method to locate certificates useful in constructing a valid CRL issuer certification path to a trust anchor.
sections.eli5: There are ways to find someone's certificate using a phone book or by following hints in other certificates. This RFC adds a hint that the CRL itself can carry.

sections.title: Authority Information Access CRL Extension
sections.content:
This section defines the use of the Authority Information Access extension in a CRL. The syntax and semantics defined in RFC 3280 for certificate extensions are also used for the CRL extension. The extension is identified by the object identifier (OID) 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.1 and uses the AuthorityInfoAccessSyntax structure.

When present in a CRL, the extension MUST include at least one AccessDescription specifying id-ad-caIssuers as the access method. Access method types other than id-ad-caIssuers MUST NOT be included. The extension MUST NOT be marked critical. At least one instance of AccessDescription SHOULD specify an access location that is an HTTP or LDAP Uniform Resource Identifier (URI).
sections.eli5: The CRL includes an address telling where to download the signer's certificate. The address can be an HTTP link or an LDAP directory location.

sections.title: Deployment and Access Methods
sections.content:
For information available via HTTP or FTP, the access location MUST be a uniform resource identifier and the URI MUST point to a file containing certificates. The certificate file MUST contain either a single Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) encoded certificate (indicated by the .cer file extension) or a collection of certificates (indicated by the .p7c file extension, a PKCS#7 certs-only CMS message as specified in RFC 2797).

For LDAP access, the access location SHOULD be a uniform resource identifier specifying a distinguished name and attribute(s), and optionally a host name. When a directoryName is used, information is obtained from a locally configured directory server. Implementations supporting directoryName access MUST be prepared to find the needed certificate in the crossCertificatePair, cACertificate, or userCertificate attributes.
sections.eli5: The address might be a website (.cer or .p7c file) or a directory system (LDAP). Computers know how to talk to both kinds of places.
